catalog_quote: In the H variety of Eastern Cham, final syllables are stressed and fully realized. All preceding syllables are unstressed and reduced. Its consonant inventory is smaller and its vowels tend to be centralized to schwa. This type of iambic stress pattern is common in Mainland Southeast Asia. ... First, while the H variety has many polysyllabic words composed of a final stressed syllable and of one or two unstressed presyllables (the presyllables are called /lang liku?/ in Cham), the L variety has lost almost all of its presyllables and has become virtually monosyllabic (Alieva 1986, 1991, 1994; Aymonier 1889; Blood 1962; Brunelle 2005a, in press; Bùi 1996; Lee 1966; Thurgood 1999). For example, the words /pat8aj/ ‘rice’ and /limɔ/ ‘cow’ are typically realized as /t8aj/ and /mɔ/ in L.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final/main-syllable stress, iambic, reduced presyllables; Brunelle 2008). Adds the historical framing (iambic final stress preceding register/tone development) but no new placement detail; snippet-level evidence only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Phan Rang (Eastern) Cham disyllables the final (main) syllable carries primary stress; the initial presyllable is unstressed, variable and often dropped, so words collapse to monosyllables; historically Chamic iambic (final-stress) words, with later register/tone development in Phan Rang Cham.

new_statements.identity_note: Thurgood treats the language as 'Phan Rang Cham' (= Eastern Cham, east2563, Ninh Thuan/Binh Thuan, Vietnam); pp. 60-63 discuss its disyllable-to-monosyllable reduction, p. 196 its tone/register system; family-level Chamic statements (p. 106) also apply.
